prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Eight cadets and staff members were killed in Pakistan during an an eight-hour standoff Monday with gunmen who stormed a police training center in Lahore, said Gen. Athar Abbas, a military spokesman. Police fire into the air after retaking the police training center in Lahore attacked by militants. The militants had been holed up on the top floor of a three-story building, said Rehman Malik, the head of the country's Interior Ministry. Security forces gained control of the first two floors and eventually made their way to the top, finally taking control of it and arresting the gunmen Monday afternoon. Television pictures showed security forces firing into the air from the roof of the building after the firefight. "The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas confirmed the figures. Abbas added some of the dead militants blew themselves up. The gang of seven gunmen stormed the academy in the Manawan area of the eastern Pakistani city, said Malik. Abbas had previously said 30 people were killed. He cited the error on wrong information by his sources at the scene.  Watch more about the attack » . At a news conference Monday night, Malik named the leader of the Pakistani Taliban, Baitullah Mehsud, and his followers as the prime suspect in organizing the attack. Mehsud is also accused of plotting the assassination of former PM Benazir Bhutto. At least 78 people were wounded in the attack, authorities said. Lahore is the same city where gunmen opened fire March 10 on a bus carrying members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team on their way to a stadium for a match. The well-coordinated attack wounded at least eight members of the team and killed a driver and six Pakistani police officers. In Monday's incident, the attackers hurled grenades, then stormed the compound and opened fire while officers were taking part in their morning drill. About 800 officers train at the facility, but authorities could not say exactly how many were inside at the time. The attackers, some in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, said Asim Rizwan, spokesman for governor of Punjab -- the province where Lahore is located. Paramilitary forces and the army descended on the scene. Every few minutes, the gunmen detonated explosives or fired on reporters and police personnel outside, sending them scurrying for cover. Angry onlookers pumped their fists in the air and cheered as police led away a suspect they had captured. He had on him a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

outputs.L2:
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — A gun battle lasting eight hours at a police academy in Lahore ended Monday with eight cadets and employees dead, according to military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas.

Rehman Malik, who heads Pakistan’s Interior Ministry, said the attackers had barricaded themselves on the uppermost level of a three-story building. Security personnel first secured the lower two floors before advancing to the third, where they regained full control and detained the surviving assailants Monday afternoon.

After the fighting ended, television footage showed police on the building’s roof shooting into the air. Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters that the operation had concluded, with four militants dead and three in custody. Malik and Abbas verified those totals, and Abbas said some of the attackers who died had detonated explosives on themselves.

Malik said the seven-member group had raided the training facility in Manawan, an area of the eastern city of Lahore. Abbas initially reported 30 fatalities but later explained that sources at the scene had provided him with incorrect information.

During a Monday night news conference, Malik identified Pakistani Taliban chief Baitullah Mehsud and his supporters as the leading suspects behind the assault. Mehsud has also been accused of planning the killing of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.

Officials said no fewer than 78 people were injured. Lahore was also the site of a March 10 shooting in which gunmen attacked a bus transporting Sri Lanka’s national cricket team to a stadium for a match. That coordinated ambush injured at least eight players and killed the bus driver along with six Pakistani police officers.

In Monday’s attack, the militants first threw grenades, then entered the compound and began shooting as officers conducted their morning exercises. Roughly 800 officers undergo training at the academy, although authorities could not determine precisely how many were present at the time.

Some attackers wore police uniforms, and they held dozens of officers captive, according to Asim Rizwan, spokesman for the governor of Punjab, the province that includes Lahore.

Army and paramilitary units arrived at the academy. At intervals of several minutes, the gunmen set off explosives or fired toward journalists and police outside, forcing them to repeatedly seek cover.

Crowds reacted with raised fists and cheers when officers escorted away one captured suspect. Officials told CNN that he was carrying a grenade and a knife.

CNN’s Reza Sayah contributed to the report.

Security forces eventually regained control of the three-story building. Four militants were killed during the operation, and three others were arrested. Pakistani officials named Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud and his followers as the leading suspects behind the assault.

The attack came only weeks after gunmen targeted Sri Lanka’s national cricket team in Lahore on March 3. Seven people were killed in that shooting, and several members of the team were wounded.
outputs.L4:
Seven heavily armed gunmen attacked a police training center on the outskirts of Lahore, Pakistan, hurling grenades and opening fire as hundreds of recruits were taking part in morning exercises. The assault sent cadets and staff scrambling for cover and triggered an eight-hour siege at the three-story complex.

Pakistani police, army units and paramilitary forces surrounded the center before moving through the building floor by floor. Gunfire and explosions continued during the operation as security personnel worked to rescue those trapped inside and regain control of the compound. When the siege ended, security forces raised the national flag from the roof to signal that the facility had been cleared.

Eight cadets and staff members were killed, and at least 78 people were wounded. Four of the attackers died during the fighting, while three others were captured. Authorities began questioning the detained suspects in an effort to determine who had organized and supported the assault.

Pakistani officials identified Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud as the prime suspect, although the investigation was still continuing. The attack highlighted the ability of militant groups to strike a major security institution in one of Pakistan’s largest cities and intensified concerns that violence rooted in the country’s tribal regions was spreading into urban centers.

**Gunmen storm police training center in Lahore, killing at least 8 officers**

**LAHORE, Pakistan —** Heavily armed gunmen stormed a police training academy outside Lahore on Monday, opening fire and throwing grenades before holding off security forces for hours, Pakistani officials said.

At least eight police personnel were killed and more than 90 people were wounded, according to government officials. Casualty figures varied during the operation and were expected to change.

The assault began during morning drills at the Manawan Police Training School, near Pakistan’s border with India. Witnesses said some attackers wore police-style uniforms and fired indiscriminately at recruits before taking positions inside the compound.

Pakistani security forces surrounded the academy and later regained control after a siege lasting several hours. Interior Ministry officials said multiple attackers were killed and several suspects were detained, though authorities were still working to determine the exact number of assailants.

Interior Minister Rehman Malik said the attackers were well trained and equipped with automatic weapons, grenades and supplies for a prolonged confrontation. Authorities had not immediately identified the group responsible.

Television footage showed police officers celebrating on the academy’s roof after the compound was secured, while ambulances transported casualties from the scene.

The attack comes amid growing concern over militant violence in Pakistan and follows a deadly assault on Sri Lanka’s cricket team in Lahore earlier that month.

An investigation is underway, officials said.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Lahore police academy attack, the security forces’ response, and the suspected involvement of Pakistani Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud.
counterfactuals.output:
On March 30, 2009, about a dozen heavily armed militants attacked the Manawan Police Training School outside Lahore while recruits were conducting morning drills. Using rifles and grenades, they seized parts of the compound and held off authorities for several hours. At least eight police personnel were killed, dozens were wounded, and casualty figures varied in early reports.

Police, Rangers, and army commandos surrounded the academy, used helicopters and rooftop positions, and eventually stormed the complex after an approximately eight-hour siege. Several attackers were killed—some reportedly by suicide explosions—and several suspects were captured.

Pakistani authorities quickly suspected Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan leader Baitullah Mehsud and allied militant networks. Mehsud subsequently claimed responsibility, saying the assault was retaliation for U.S. drone strikes in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Although investigators examined possible links to other Punjab-based extremist groups, his claim and the attackers’ apparent connections to the tribal militant network made the Pakistani Taliban the principal suspect.
